Article Title: Nepal floods revive Bihar’s annual nightmare: Why the state faces flooding every year
Article Text:
The rivers that sustain the region for most of the year turn dangerous during the monsoon

What was the trigger this time?

Why does Bihar drown every year?

Class I refers to flash floods, which occur due to rainfall in Nepal, have a short lead time of around eight hours between forecast and flood, and recede quickly.

Class II refers to river floods, with a lead time of 24 hours and floodwaters that take a week or more to recede.

Class III refers to drainage congestion at river confluences, where the lead time exceeds 24 hours and the water lasts the entire monsoon season, receding only after about three months.

Class IV refers to permanently waterlogged areas.

Embankments: Solution or part of the problem?

Everybody loves a good flood

The traditions around floods

NEW DELHI: Boats replacing cars on flooded roads, families moving to relief camps and swollen rivers spilling into villages. North Bihar is bracing for familiar scenes once again as floodwaters from Nepal move downstream.Floods have long been a part of life in northern Bihar. But a growing population and rapid urbanisation have made their impact more severe over the years.The rivers that sustain the region for most of the year turn dangerous during the monsoon. And for people living here, there is little choice but to face the floods, rebuild and prepare for the cycle to repeat itself.Bihar minister Ramkripal Yadav said the state government is closely monitoring the flood threat in Bihar in view of the tragedy in Nepal."Bihar is adjacent to Nepal, and the water that has come from Nepal in the past has affected many areas of Bihar, leading to loss of life and property, destruction of crops and homes. The Bihar government and the chief minister himself are monitoring this," Yadav told ANI.He assured that the state government will extend every possible help to those affected."The Bihar government will provide every possible help. The flood victims of Bihar have the first right on Bihar's treasury, and it is secure for them.The government will work," he added.A glacial collapse at the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 triggered a flash flood in Nepal that has claimed more than 600 lives.Analysis of satellite imagery indicated that a large mass of ice and rock may have fallen into the Lende Khola river, temporarily blocking its flow and creating a natural dam that later breached, sending floodwaters downstream.Due to the collapse, a large volume of ice and rock debris entered the Lende Khola, a tributary of the Bhote Koshi river in Nepal, generating a sudden surge that carried water, sediment and large boulders downstream.The scale of the devastation can be gauged from the fact that twelve hydropower plants were reportedly knocked offline, dozens of bridges were swept away and the only road connecting the valley to the rest of Nepal was destroyed.Nature could not care less about political borders. And a flood that originated in Nepal will not stop at the border. From Nepal, the floodwaters will eventually move into north Bihar, before flowing into West Bengal and eventually Bangladesh, where they will empty into the sea.Speaking to The Times of India, IIT-trained civil engineer and flood expert Dinesh Mishra said Bihar's locational disadvantage is one of the reasons why it drowns every year in floods. He said the state is situated in such a way that water comes directly through the south-flowing rivers from Nepal."The first reason is Bihar's locational disadvantage. Bihar is situated in such a way that water comes directly from the mountains," Mishra said."All the rivers that enter Bihar from Nepal are south-flowing. So, the area north of the Ganga will inevitably remain waterlogged. And if it does not, there will be drought in the region," he added.Rivers originating from the Himalayas, like Kosi, Gandak, Burhi Gandak and Bagmati, carry huge volumes of silt with them to Bihar. When the water level increases due to rain, these rivers overflow their banks.This makes Bihar India's most flood-prone state, with 76 per cent of the population in north Bihar living under the threat of floods.Bihar's disaster management authority classifies floods into four categories.This year, according to Bihar water resources department, the Gandak river has crossed the danger mark in Gopalganj, while the barrage at Valmikinagar released around 99,800 cusecs of water at 8 pm on Saturday."The water level of several rivers, including the Gandak, Kosi, Burhi Gandak and the Ganga, has been rising. Incessant rainfall in the catchment areas of Nepal has led to rivers touching or flowing above the danger level at several places," a senior official of the water resources department said.People in West Champaran, East Champaran, Sitamarhi and Muzaffarpur, besides Gopalganj, Saran and Vaishali, have also been facing heightened fears over the past three days following an unprecedented inflow of water from Nepal.Other than flooding, another concern is soil erosion along the banks of swollen rivers.For over a century, embankments along rivers have been a major preventive measure against floods. Successive governments built these walls along river banks to prevent rivers from deviating from their course and protect settlements.However, Dinesh Mishra said these embankments are the root cause of the havoc wreaked by floods rather than being the solution."You build embankments basically to prevent river water from spilling out. But if floodwater that would naturally flow into the river is stopped, the water has nowhere to go," Mishra said."If it cannot return to the river, it will move into areas that were previously not affected by floods," he added.Mishra said Kosi once had space to spread and deposit its sediments, but embankments have now confined the river. With the sediments having nowhere to go, the riverbed has been rising, making the Kosi increasingly prone to overflowing."The river carries silt with it, and because of the embankments, the riverbed continues to rise," he said.Interestingly, Flood Atlas of Bihar, prepared by Isro along with the central and state governments, also says that "there must be a realisation that minimising the risk and damage from floods may be a more rational way of flood management rather than formulating structural measures along the dynamic rivers such as the Kosi."During the conversation, Mishra, however, rejected the notion that floods have always been a source of sorrow for Bihar. He said floods are also a time of celebration.He said farmers eagerly wait for floods because, as he put it, "a fresh layer of silt is deposited on the fields after floods, making the soil more fertile."He added that in the remote villages of north Bihar, people sometimes wait for floods because relief funds and the attention of politicians are also drawn towards villages where little development work has been done."People have been made this way. Earlier, they had clear SOPs to protect themselves during floods. But now, because they have become dependent on the government for relief, lives are lost," he said.For generations, floods in north Bihar were not simply seen as a force to be feared. They were woven into the rhythm of life, with people learning to live alongside the rivers rather than trying to keep them at bay."Our ancestors knew this was a water-rich, flood-prone region. When they settled here, they must have done so with that understanding," Mishra said.The relationship with the rivers was deeply personal. People revered them as mothers, and when the rains failed, women in villages would perform rituals to invoke the rivers and call for water.But when the floodwaters refused to recede, another ritual would follow. Women would gather with fruits, flowers, sandalwood, akshat and sindoor to persuade the river to leave.The rivers were considered unmarried, Mishra said, and women would even "threaten" them with marriage if they refused to listen.These traditions show how closely floods have been tied to life in north Bihar for generations.People did not always see the rivers only as a threat. They depended on them for water, fertile soil and agriculture, even as they feared the destruction that came when the rivers overflowed.That relationship continues even today. Every monsoon, the same rivers bring both relief and anxiety. And once the water recedes, people clean their homes, return to their fields and begin rebuilding knowing that the floods may return the next year.
Article Summary: A glacial collapse at the Nepal-Tibet border on August 26 triggered a flash flood in Nepal that has claimed more than 600 lives. Bihar minister Ramkripal Yadav said the state government is closely monitoring the flood threat in Bihar in view of the tragedy in Nepal.

Article Text:

PM Modi attends yoga session in Tashkent

PM Modi's engagements in Uzbekistan

PM Modi to travel to Kyrgyzstan for SCO summit

NEW DELHI: India and Uzbekistan on Sunday agreed to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence and energy as Prime Minister Narendra Modi held delegation-level talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Tashkent, with the two sides seeking to advance their strategic partnership and shared development goals.PM Modi, who is on a two-day state visit to Uzbekistan from August 29 to 30 at the invitation of Mirziyoyev, received a ceremonial welcome before the two leaders held talks on strengthening bilateral ties. The discussions focused on key areas of mutual interest and ways to advance the shared developmental visions of 'Viksit Bharat' and 'Yangi Uzbekistan', according to the Indian side.The talks came as India and Uzbekistan looked to build on the significant progress made in their strategic partnership in recent years. PM Modi had earlier said the relationship had witnessed significant advancement and expressed his desire to further deepen cooperation in key sectors.Earlier on Sunday, PM Modi attended a yoga session hosted by the Yoga Federation of Uzbekistan, highlighting the growing people-to-people and cultural ties between the two countries."Yoga has immense appeal in Uzbekistan. It is bringing people and cultures together and strengthening people-to-people ties between India and Uzbekistan," the Ministry of External Affairs said in a post on X.After the session, PM Modi said Uzbekistan had been a "proud participant" in the first-ever World Yogasana Championship held in Ahmedabad earlier this year. He also noted that some of the medal winners from the championship were present at the yoga session.PM Modi arrived in Tashkent on Saturday and was warmly received by Mirziyoyev at the airport. Following his arrival, the prime minister visited Yangi Uzbekistan Park and laid a wreath at the Independence Monument along with the Uzbek president.He later interacted with members of the Indian community at a hotel in Tashkent. The programme featured Kathak and Andijan Polka performances by members of the diaspora, while Uzbek children performed to the Indian song "Ude Jab Jab Zulfe Teri".The prime minister also watched a fusion performance featuring the tabla alongside traditional Uzbek instruments Doira and Chang, underlining the cultural links between the two countries.After concluding his Uzbekistan visit, PM Modi is scheduled to travel from Tashkent to Kyrgyzstan to participate in the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation summit on August 31 and September 1 at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov.The summit will mark the 25th anniversary of the SCO. PM Modi is expected to address the gathering and highlight India's priorities of "Security, Connectivity and Opportunity".He will also hold bilateral meetings with leaders of SCO member countries on the sidelines of the summit.PM Modi is further scheduled to attend the opening ceremony of the sixth World Nomad Games.The Uzbekistan visit is PM Modi's fourth trip to the Central Asian country and comes as New Delhi seeks to expand its engagement with the region through greater economic, strategic, energy and connectivity cooperation.
Article Summary: India and Uzbekistan agree to deepen cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence and energy. Prime Minister Narendra Modi held delegation-level talks with Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev in Tashkent. PM Modi is on a two-day state visit to Uzbekistan from August 29 to 30.

Article Title: ‘No question of bringing back Article 370’: BJP hits out at Mirwaiz Umar Farooq
Article Text:
Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, chief cleric of Kashmir, was criticized by the BJP's Jammu and Kashmir unit

NEW DELHI: BJP Jammu and Kashmir spokesperson Altaf Thakur on Sunday rejected Kashmir's chief cleric chairman Mirwaiz Umar Farooq 's call for political parties to unite for the restoration of Article 370 , saying there was "no question" of bringing back the constitutional provision.Thakur said Parliament had taken a "historic" constitutional decision to abrogate Article 370 and that the Supreme Court had subsequently upheld it. He accused the Mirwaiz of making statements that could disturb the peace that has returned to the Valley after years of violence."Mirwaiz Umar Farooq needs to realize that Article 370 will not be reinstated. No political party, leader, or pressure group can undo the fundamental truth that Parliament has permanently buried Article 370," Thakur said.He said attempts to revive the issue risked pushing Kashmir back into a period of political instability."These kinds of statements are intended to incite people and disturb the tranquility of the Valley once more. This will never be permitted. The return of peace to Kashmir has come at a very high cost to the country. Thakur stated, "We cannot allow politically motivated statements to undermine or challenge the sacrifices made by our courageous security forces and civilians, including political workers who gave their lives for peace and democracy.Thakur said people in Kashmir should not be pushed into another cycle of violence, shutdowns and unrest after having endured years of disruption."Those who try to resurrect old fault lines need to realize that Kashmir has progressed. Our young people are looking for the chances to educate themselves, work, entrepreneurship, investment, and travel. "They don't want to go back to a time, when violence dictated the future and shutdown calendars controlled their lives," he added in the statement.Thakur said political parties were free to express their views within the Constitution, but argued that repeatedly seeking reversal of a constitutional decision upheld by the Supreme Court was futile."Democracy gives the right to speak and participate, but democracy cannot be reduced to repeatedly demanding the reversal of a constitutional decision that has already been upheld by the highest court of the country," he stated.He also reiterated the BJP's position that statehood for Jammu and Kashmir would be restored at an appropriate time, while insisting that statehood and Article 370 were separate issues."Statehood and Article 370 are clearly different. The government has declared that statehood would be restored at a suitable moment. However, there is no way that Article 370 could be reinstated,". "Those who are causing confusion on this matter need are advised to stop misleading the public," he stated.Earlier, Mirwaiz had criticised the National Conference government's performance, saying its current position differed from commitments made during the 2024 Assembly elections."The people's rights have been taken away, Jammu & Kashmir has been split, and all of our legal and constitutional obligations have been totally disregarded," he said.While acknowledging that issues such as electricity, roads and development were important, Mirwaiz said they were secondary to what he described as the broader question concerning the status of Jammu and Kashmir.“ But I think these are secondary issues. The real issue is that the very existence of the people of Jammu & Kashmir is under threat. At this juncture, all political parties in J&K should not only raise their voice for the restoration of statehood but also seek the restoration of Article 370, which was the basis accession (with India),” he stated.Mirwaiz also alleged that the Union government had broken its commitments to the people of Jammu and Kashmir dating back to 1947, including constitutional guarantees.
Article Summary: Mirwaiz Umar Farooq, chief cleric of Kashmir, criticized by the BJP's Jammu and Kashmir unit. Thakur said attempts to revive the issue risked pushing Kashmir back into a period of political instability. He accused the Mirwaiz of making statements that could disturb the peace that has returned to the Valley.

Article Title: 1 in 5 food samples fails: Why so few cases end in conviction
Article Text:
Inadequate packaging can increase the risk of contamination

Food safety checks expose widespread violations

UP finds highest share of violations

Enforcement gaps raise concerns over food safety

Testing reveals gaps in India’s food safety system

Staff shortage adds to enforcement challenge

Shortages in food safety staff hamper monitoring and enforcement.

Milk, dairy among frequently flagged foods

Milk and dairy products among food samples that continue to fail safety standards.

NEW DELHI: Nearly one in five food samples tested across India was found to be non-conforming in 2025-26, even as only 4.8% of food safety violations ended in convictions, highlighting gaps in enforcement and staffing across states, according to data analysed by Richa Gandhi.The share of non-conforming food samples has remained around 20% over the past five years, despite a steady rise in the number of samples tested. In 2025-26, authorities analysed 2,23,808 samples, of which 40,023 were found to be non-conforming.The proportion of non-conforming samples stood at 17.9% in 2025-26, down from 20.2% in 2024-25 and 19.8% in 2023-24. It had peaked at 25.1% in 2022-23.At the same time, the conviction rate has gradually increased, rising from 2% in 2021-22 to 4.8% in 2025-26. However, monetary penalties remain the more common form of action against violators.Uttar Pradesh recorded the highest proportion of non-conforming samples among the states listed, with 52% of the nearly 40,000 samples tested in 2025-26 found to be non-conforming.The state analysed 39,519 samples and found 20,021 to be non-conforming.Haryana followed with 31%, while Jharkhand recorded 28%, Rajasthan 27%, Puducherry 22% and Himachal Pradesh 20%.Tamil Nadu analysed the highest number of samples among the larger states, with nearly 45,000 tests, and also recorded the highest conviction rate among those states.Chandigarh recorded the highest conviction rate overall at 32.1%, followed by Tamil Nadu at 21.5%, Kerala at 17.7%, Haryana at 16% and Delhi at 14.7%.The data points to a sharp gap between the scale of food safety violations detected through testing and the number of cases that ultimately result in convictions.Shortages in food safety personnel are another major constraint on monitoring and enforcement.Bihar has the largest gap among the states listed, with 91 of its 105 sanctioned food safety posts vacant. Jharkhand has 74 vacancies against 77 sanctioned posts, while Chhattisgarh has 70 vacancies against 125 posts.Andhra Pradesh has 68 vacancies out of 145 sanctioned posts, followed by Uttarakhand with 65 vacancies out of 57 sanctioned posts, according to the data.Haryana has 57 vacancies against 367 sanctioned posts, while Odisha has 57 vacancies against 147. Tripura has 52 vacancies against 23 sanctioned posts, Manipur 50 against 34 and Sikkim 50 against four.The staffing gaps limit the ability of state authorities to regularly inspect establishments, collect samples and pursue violations through the enforcement process.Milk and dairy products, ghee, spices, edible oils and sweets remain among the food categories frequently flagged in regulatory actions and recent cases.In one major case, ghee supplied for the preparation of Tirupati laddus came under scrutiny after samples failed quality tests amid allegations of adulteration with vegetable oils and animal fats.Milk and milk products such as paneer and khoya have also faced increased scrutiny. The Food Safety and Standards Authority of India ordered a nationwide crackdown between September and October following cases involving alleged detergent and urea adulteration in Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra.In Punjab, 47% of milk, cheese and dairy samples reportedly failed tests over a three-year period. Cheese was identified as particularly vulnerable to adulteration involving starch and chemical additives, with 255 of 531 samples failing tests in 2024-25 alone.Spices such as turmeric and chilli powder have also been the subject of seizures over adulteration involving synthetic colours, wood dust and other unsafe fillers.Edible oils are another concern, with cheaper palm oil being used to adulterate more expensive oils such as groundnut and mustard oil.Sweets and khoya are also regularly identified as high-risk categories in FSSAI advisories during festive periods, when demand rises sharply.The figures underline the challenge facing India's food safety system: while testing has expanded and the detection of violations remains significant, limited staffing and the relatively low rate of convictions continue to constrain enforcement.
Article Summary: Nearly one in five food samples tested across India was found to be non- conforming in 2025-26. Only 4.8% of food safety violations ended in convictions, according to data analysed by Richa Gandhi. Shortages in food safety staff hamper monitoring and enforcement.

Article Title: NEET-PG 2026 exam at Jaipur centre rescheduled to September 5 over power outage
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: The NEET-PG 2026 examination at a Jaipur centre has been rescheduled to September 5 after concerns over a power outage and technical disruptions during the test on Sunday, according to National Board of Examinations in Medical Sciences (NBEMS) sources.The examination at iON Digital Zone Sitapura 2 in Jaipur will be reconducted for all candidates allotted to the centre. Nearly 300 candidates were scheduled to appear for the examination there.NBEMS sources said further details regarding the rescheduled examination would be communicated separately to the affected candidates.The development came as candidates at two iON Digital Zone centres in Sitapura reported technical disruptions during the NEET-PG examination.According to news agency PTI, candidates alleged that the examination started late and computer systems repeatedly shut down after the test began.Some candidates claimed their systems went down six to seven times during the examination, while others alleged that the disruption occurred even more frequently. They said that after the systems restarted, only a few questions appeared on some computers before they went down again.Several candidates came out of the examination centre amid the disruption and staged a protest, questioning the technical arrangements.They also raised concerns about whether the technical failures could affect the fairness of the examination and demanded an impartial inquiry.A candidate, Gunjan, said aspirants paid a substantial fee for an important examination such as NEET-PG but were not provided adequate technical infrastructure for an uninterrupted test.Candidates said many aspirants had prepared for the examination for one to two years and feared that the disruptions could affect their future.Police and administration officials reached the centre following the protest. ACP Jaipur South Lalit Sharma said police were deployed at the spot to maintain law and order amid the commotion.Meanwhile, the NEET-PG 2026 examination commenced across the country on Sunday, with more than 2.73 lakh medical graduates appearing for the postgraduate medical entrance examination at designated centres.The examination was conducted by NBEMS in computer-based mode in a single shift from 9 am to 12:30 pm.NEET-PG is held for admission to postgraduate medical courses across the country.
Article Summary: NEET-PG 2026 examination at a Jaipur centre has been rescheduled to September 5. Concerns over a power outage and technical disruptions during the test on Sunday. Nearly 300 candidates were scheduled to appear for the examination there.

Article Title: 'Drug-free India' to 'vocal for local': Key quotes from PM Modi’s 137th Mann Ki Baat
Article Text:
PM Modi highlights 'BharatRajya' website in 137th edition of 'Mann Ki Baat ', calls for collective push towards 'Drug-Free India'

Top quotes from the episode

The campaign ‘Drug-Free Youth for Developed India’ is rapidly gaining momentum across the country. Its objective is absolutely clear: a drug-free youth, a drug-free India. Drug addiction does not engulf only one person. Its consequences are also suffered by the entire family and society. I would appreciate those who raise awareness among others against drugs and come forward to help people struggling with addiction.

In the month of August, we see many colours of patriotism everywhere. From National Handloom Day and the anniversary of the Quit India Movement to Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, these occasions make the month special. The Har Ghar Tiranga campaign strengthens this feeling further. This year has become even more special because 150 years of Vande Mataram are being completed.”

PM SVANidhi scheme is giving new strength to millions of such mothers and sisters. This aspect of women’s empowerment does not receive as much discussion as it should. Around 46 per cent of the beneficiaries of PM SVANidhi are women. That means nearly 35 lakh women across the country are connected with this scheme and are taking their businesses forward.

This year, we saw a similarly inspiring picture of cleanliness and public participation during the Shri Amarnath Yatra. Thousands of sanitation workers remained engaged in service day and night on difficult routes. More than 400 metric tonnes of waste was collected and processed during the pilgrimage this year. One aspect of this effort particularly pleased me.

Vaishalu Puroji from Phek district of Nagaland began growing flowers on a small scale. Gradually, she began to see an opportunity in it. During this journey, she received training in scientific flower cultivation from the local Krishi Vigyan Kendra. She then planted thousands of gladiolus plants on just one-quarter of an acre of land. More than 5,000 flowers bloomed in her very first attempt.

Today, the dreams of our daughters are travelling from the Earth all the way into space. And you will be proud to know that India is bringing together thousands of girls from across the world who dream of achieving such things. The name of this effort is Mission ShaktiSAT. Through it, 12,000 female students from 108 countries are getting an opportunity to learn satellite technology and move forward in the field of innovation.”

During this festive season, I once again repeat my appeal for Vocal for Local. And Vocal for Local does not simply mean buying earthen lamps. Its vision is much broader. Whatever we buy for our homes, let us check once whether it has been made in India. I appeal to you to adopt Vocal for Local yourself and also inspire others to do the same.

NEW DELHI: In the 137th episode of Mann Ki Baat , Prime Minister Narendra Modi highlighted grassroots initiatives and individuals creating change through technology, social action, entrepreneurship and community participation. He began by discussing a digital initiative by Mumbai-based Krishna Sheshadri that uses technology to make Indian history more engaging.PM Modi then called for greater public participation in the campaign for a drug-free India, particularly among young people.He also spoke about the patriotic spirit surrounding August, including Har Ghar Tiranga, National Handloom Day, the Quit India Movement anniversary, Partition Horrors Remembrance Day, Independence Day and National Space Day.He highlighted women street vendors benefiting from PM SVANidhi, citing examples from Ghaziabad and Bengaluru.Cleanliness was another major theme, with PM Modi highlighting young volunteers in Uttar Pradesh and sanitation efforts during the Amarnath Yatra. He then showcased individuals turning personal interests and environmental conservation into livelihoods, including a flower farmer in Nagaland and women involved in ecotourism and forest conservation in Odisha.The Prime Minister also highlighted Mission ShaktiSAT, which is bringing thousands of girls from across the world into satellite technology and innovation. He discussed the growing cultivation of avocado by Indian farmers, paid tribute to Bengali cinema icon Uttam Kumar ahead of his birth centenary, and ended by speaking about Janmashtami, Vishwakarma Puja, Diwali and the importance of buying Indian-made products under the Vocal for Local campaign.

Article Title: Tilak Varma in India’s ODI World Cup plans as selectors seek Shreyas Iyer backup
Article Text:
India's Shreyas Iyer, center, with batting partner Tilak Varma (AP/PTI)

Selectors wary of moving batters around

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Team for Afg series likely by Sept 3

New Delhi: India’s team management and selectors are working on backups for the middle order ahead of the ODI World Cup next year. TOI has learnt that Tilak Varma’s name has come up as a potential backup option for Shreyas Iyer in the top six of the batting lineup.Tilak, being a left-handed batter, is seen as someone who can break the monotony of right-handers in the batting lineup. Tilak has been asked to work on his bowling since it is believed that his off-breaks have a lot of potential. The team management, in fact, has flagged the dearth of bowling options in the top order, citing it as a reason for extra pressure on the lower order and the bowlers.The planning for the ODI World Cup will only begin in earnest when India reach New Zealand in October, since most of the first-choice players will not be available for the ODI series against West Indies at home from September 27. A full-strength T20 team is also scheduled to travel to Japan for the Asian Games at the same time.“Head coach Gautam Gambhir and captain Shubman Gill feel there isn’t any backup ready for the middle order. With Hardik Pandya and Nitish Kumar Reddy being prone to injuries, they want someone in the top order who can at least chip in with four overs in an ODI,” a BCCI source said.Over the last year, the team management has been compelled to play either Washington Sundar or Axar Patel at No.5 or No. 6 to balance the playing XI. In the last series in England, Ishan Kishan was sent in ahead of vice-captain Iyer.“The team has to be prepared for conditions in South Africa in the World Cup. Iyer got injured in Australia and his game against pace and bounce is untested of late. The team already has two ageing players in Rohit Sharma and Virat Kohli. They are having niggles as well. KL Rahul too will be over 35 by the time the World Cup comes around. Ravindra Jadeja isn’t a certainty either. The fielding of the team has suffered due to fitness issues. The team management feels that they need younger backups ready,” the source said.The selectors, it is learnt, are not comfortable with playing batters out of position. Last year, Ruturaj Gaikwad was played at No. 4 and scored a hundred against South Africa in Raipur. But he has not been picked in the ODI team since.“Gaikwad was picked as backup opener since Gill was injured. The team management feels Tilak could have been tried in that place. That’s why they don’t want to rush Devdutt Padikkal in the ODI setup because he found his calling in white-ball cricket while opening the batting,” the source said.The team for the West Indies series, however, will be an anomaly since Iyer, Tilak, Ishan and Axar will not be available. NEW DELHI: The humble pinch of hing used in Indian kitchens has come under the scanner, with the Food Safety and Standards Authority of India (FSSAI) issuing prohibition orders against Everest Food Products Private Limited and Laljee Godhoo and Company over non-compliance in compounded hing and asafoetida products. In a social media post, the food regulator said it had issued prohibition orders against the two companies under the Food Safety and Standards Act, 2006. Article Title: ‘Frustrated’ Delhi man murders schizophrenic son, 2 held
Article Text:
Talukdar Ansari and his friend Mohammad Wasim alias Akram

Man, friend kill son with mental illness





NEW DELHI: A 64-year-old man and his friend have been arrested for allegedly killing the man’s 38-year-old son by assaulting him with a stone and strangling him in southeast Delhi’s Kalindi Kunj.Talukdar Ansari told police that his son, who was schizophrenic, had become aggressive and he was frustrated by his behaviour. Ansari also said he couldn’t arrange for his son’s treatment, investigators said.Ansari’s friend has been identified as Mohammad Wasim alias Akram (49). Both work as tailors. The deceased was Gul Hasan, said police.On Aug 23, police were informed around 7.13pm about the body of an unidentified man lying inside an abandoned container near the NTPC wall in Kalindi Kunj.The spot was around 500 metres east of Delhi-Mumbai Expressway.Police personnel who went to the site spotted an injury mark on the man’s head, while a concrete stone with apparent bloodstains was found nearby. murder case was registered and joint CP Vijay Kumar formed teams under the supervision of DCP Vineet Kumar.After several days of analysis of CCTV camera footage, investigators traced the movements of the victim, later identified as Hasan, and found him travelling with two men towards the crime scene.The two men were subsequently traced to a stitching factory in southeast Delhi’s Govindpuri. Ansari and Wasim were apprehended Friday afternoon by a team led by ACP Anil Sharma and comprising station house officer Raman Kumar and others.Ansari claimed that Hasan was suffering from mental health problems, which police described as schizophrenia. Ansari allegedly said Hasan had even attacked him and other family members.“He also told us that he was not able to get him proper treatment. So he, along with his friend, made the plan a few days ago,” police said.According to investigators, they took Hasan to the abandoned container on the pretext of taking him to a doctor.Once they reached the secluded location, Wasim allegedly struck him with a stone, following which Ansari also assaulted him. Hasan was then strangled with a rope made from cloth waste and the body was left there, police said.Inquiry revealed that they initially planned to push Hasan into the Yamuna , but abandoned it after finding people around when they reached the river.On the way to the isolated spot, Ansari bought samosas to keep Hasan engaged and unsuspecting.Police said they had recovered the concrete stone and the rope used in the murder and bloodstained clothes worn during the incident.
Article Summary: Talukdar Ansari told police that his son, who was schizophrenic, had become aggressive and he was frustrated by his behaviour. Ansari’s friend has been identified as Mohammad Wasim alias Akram (49). Both work as tailors, said police.

CHHATRAPATI SAMBHAJINAGAR: Cockroach Janta Party founder Abhijeet Dipke on Saturday challenged govt to file “not one but 100 cases” against him if exposing poor conditions in zilla parishad schools was a crime, insisting that FIRs would not stop his School Theek Karo (fix the schools) campaign.During visits to zilla parishad schools at Lohgaon and Karanjala in Hingoli taluka, Dipke inspected classrooms, benches, drinking water facilities and material used for preparing mid-day meals.Villagers and social activist Munir Pathan accompanied him and highlighted problems faced by students and staff.Dipke said he has been touring govt schools across Maharashtra to draw attention to inadequate infrastructure and other shortcomings.“Is it a crime to visit schools and point out the problems and lack of facilities there? Article Title: Samay Raina in soup again over remarks on people from Bihar, Kashmiri Pandits: 'They get publicity for free'

MUMBAI: Comedian Samay Raina released another episode of India's Got Latent, Season 2, on Friday, with parts of the show later circulating on social media.The episode has drawn attention over alleged remarks about people from Bihar and Kashmiri Pandits made during an interaction involving Raina and stand-up comedian Sharon Verma.The exchange began when Samay introduced Sharon to the audience in his usual style, making a joke about her Bihar background. He said, “She is from Bihar. She is so Bihari; she thinks ‘ebola’ means someone said something.”Sharon responded with a joke targeting Samay’s Kashmiri roots, telling him, “Samay is so Kashmiri; he loves getting stoned.”Samay continued the banter, adding, “Sharon Verma is a Bihari who came to Mumbai in search of a job. Just Bihari things.”Sharon then said, “At least, I left my state by my choice.” BJP MLA Ram Kadam criticised the alleged remarks and said they were made for publicity."There are certain forces in society that deliberately make controversial statements simply to gain publicity. Their sole objective is to become famous. We need to understand that the deities of Sanatan Hinduism and Kashmiri Pandits cannot be treated as subjects of ridicule.""Someone cannot deliberately do something offensive and then simply apologize afterwards. In the meantime, they get the publicity they wanted across the country for free," he added further again.Shiv Sena leader Sanjay Nirupam said comedian Raina’s show should be viewed as a comedy programme and that humour should generally be taken in that spirit.However, Nirupam said he was uncomfortable with remarks related to Bihar and a subsequent comment about Kashmir made by a woman associated with the show.“I know the remark related to Bihar wasn't good, and the way the girl connected to Bihar gave a sharp retort in the context of Kashmir, didn't sit well with me either,” Nirupam said.He said the comment appeared to touch upon the atrocities faced by Kashmiri Pandits and that Raina’s reaction also did not sit well with him.“The atrocities committed against Kashmiri Pandits - she, in some way, commented on those atrocities, and Samay Raina, who is a Kashmiri Pandit, was clapping for it. That didn't sit well with me either,” he said.Reacting to the alleged remarks, a Kashmiri Pandit said, "Look, there is no need to give too much importance to whatever conversation Samay Raina had.""It was a comedy show, and it can be called a comedy show. If I am a Kashmiri Pandit, I have the right to travel anywhere in the world; it is our fundamental right.""Similarly, if someone from Bihar goes to Bombay, it is their fundamental right. They can go anywhere in the country and live anywhere for employment or any other reason.""Now, regarding the conversation they had with each other, when you go to a comedy show, jokes keep happening. One should not take it personally, nor should it be given so much importance as to who said what to whom," he added.Another Kashmiri Pandit said, "There is a comedian named Samay Raina. He is a good man. You have seen him. We respect him and we are proud of him.""Comedians say such things, but there are other things behind them. You talked about migration but migration did not happen. They were forced to migrate.""I said that the way a comedian talks is different. It depends on the way a person thinks and how he takes it," he added.The episode also featured actress and television personality Archana Puran Singh and social media personality Orhan Awatramani, popularly known as Orry, on the panel.During the show, Raina also took a dig at Archana while speaking to a contestant.A contestant named AR Tiwari performed Bhojpuri shayari on the show. When Raina asked him what he did apart from shayari, the contestant said he also danced, vlogged and rapped.Raina then used the mention of vlogging to joke about Archana, who regularly shares family vlogs.He told the contestant, "Did you say vlog? Vlogging doesn't need talent".Archana was quick to respond.Giving Raina a sharp comeback, she said, "gaaliyan dena talent hai? (abusing is talent)."Her response was met with cheers from the audience, while Raina did not immediately have a comeback.The latest episode comes amid renewed attention on India's Got Latent, with clips from the show frequently being shared and discussed on social media.
Article Summary: Comedian Samay Raina released another episode of India's Got Latent, Season 2, on Friday. The episode has drawn attention over alleged remarks about people from Bihar and Kashmiri Pandits made during an interaction involving Raina and stand-up comedian Sharon Verma.

Article Title: 'If any Hindu thinks there should be no Muslims in India, he's not Hindu': RSS' Mohan Bhagwat in US
Article Text:

NEW DELHI: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat on Saturday said Hinduism believes in the unity of humanity, asserting that “If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in India, then he's not a Hindu.”Addressing the ‘One World One Humanity’ event in New York, Bhagwat said different religions may follow different paths, but humanity and truth remain one.“We come from a society that believes humanity is one. If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in India, then he's not a Hindu….” the RSS chief said.“If you want call yourself hindu than you must believe that all paths are leading to the same. And every human has a dignity. There is no difference between human beings,” he added.Bhagwat said diversity must be protected while stressing the importance of unity. “Diversity has to be protected as it is the rule of nature and 'Unity is universal truth,” he said.“I am not a religious scholar, nor a religious authority like you, but I am working in a society which traditionally says that religions might be different, but humanity is one. Truth is one, and humanity is a product of that truth. So humanity is one,” Bhagwat said.He added that while truth is one, it can be described in different ways depending on how people perceive it.“That truth is one truth, but it is described in many ways according to the describer. Because as human beings, we are prisoners of the software that has been created in our heads,” he said.“There are many religions, and in today's world, religions are largely defined by rituals. And to fit in a religious discipline, and to treat that path to divinity, this discipline of rituals is also necessary,” he added.The RSS chief framed his address around the idea of “oneness”, drawing parallels between the pluralism associated with the United States and what he described as Bharat’s “unity in diversity”.“When we say America, United States of America, one word is often discussed frequently. That is pluralism,” Bhagwat said. “And when we say Bharat, another word, another phrase is discussed: unity in diversity.”“For Bharat, this unity and diversity, both are in their DNA,” he said.Read more: 'RSS vision is to see the world as one' - Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat at New York event The event was organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue (AHEAD) and was described as a “landmark Raksha Bandhan gathering”.“The event carries a timeless and universal message: 'The world is one family'. It calls upon us to look beyond artificial divisions and differences, recognise the bonds that unite humanity, and embrace a spirit of mutual respect, harmony, and oneness,” the organisation said.The programme featured cultural presentations and keynote addresses centred on universal oneness and the Hindu philosophy of ‘Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam’, or the world is one family.Bhagwat arrived in the US earlier this week as part of the RSS's centenary-year global outreach programme, which also includes visits to Canada and the UK.During his visit, he has met members of the Indian diaspora, Indian-American business leaders and community representatives.Ahead of his Madison Square Garden address, images of Bhagwat were projected on billboards in New York's Times Square, carrying the words “Resolve, Harmony and Dialogue”.Bhagwat also visited the Bhakti Centre and the ISKCON temple in New York. At the temple, he participated in a food distribution initiative for homeless people and spoke about the role of Krishna consciousness in addressing conflicts and divisions.Before, the RSS had said that the Madison Square Garden event was being organised in the spirit of open dialogue and invited “anyone interested” in learning more about the organisation to participate.
Article Summary: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat said Hinduism believes in the unity of humanity. He said different religions may follow different paths, but humanity and truth remain one. “If any Hindu thinks that there should be no Muslims in India, then he's not a Hindu,” he said.

Article Title: Indian Standard Time to become mandatory for all entities from March 2027
Article Text:
Govt notifies Legal Metrology (IST) Rules, 2026, making IST mandatory for all legal, commercial and administrative activities from March 2027.

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: From March next year, all entities in India will be required to use Indian Standard Time (IST) for legal, commercial, digital and administrative activities, with govt on Saturday notifying the Legal Metrology (Indian Standard Time) Rules, 2026.The rules, notified under the Legal Metrology Act, will come into force 180 days after their publication in Gazette, making IST mandatory from around March 2027. Violations of the rules will attract penalties under the Act.The notification makes IST the mandatory time reference for all legal, administrative and official documents unless specifically exempted. It also makes IST the standard time reference across commerce, transport, public administration, legal contracts and financial operations.Entities will not be allowed to use, display or record any time reference other than IST for official purposes, except where foreign time zones are clearly labelled or where alternative time sources are permitted for scientific research, navigation or astronomy.The rules are significant as modern digital infrastructure depends on microsecond-level timing accuracy. Payment systems, stock exchanges, telecom networks, 5G services, digital navigation, power grids and data centres require synchronised clocks to authenticate transactions, coordinate operations and maintain network reliability.The notification establishes a nationwide system for time synchronisation, traceability and cybersecurity, recognising accurate time as critical digital infrastructure. Under the rules, CSIR-National Physical Laboratory (NPL) will continue to maintain India’s primary time scale, UTC(NPLI), from which IST is derived, while Regional Reference Standards Laboratories (RRSLs), ISRO’s NavIC and other authorised timing sources will disseminate official time.Another major feature of the rules is the focus on cyber resilience. Organisations must deploy proper time-synchronisation systems, protect networks against spoofing, jamming and cyberattacks, integrate multiple authorised timing sources and maintain contingency mechanisms, including atomic clocks where necessary, to ensure uninterrupted operations.
Article Summary: Govt notifies Legal Metrology (IST) Rules, 2026, making IST mandatory for all legal, commercial and administrative activities from March 2027. Violations of the rules will attract penalties under the Act. The rules are significant as modern digital infrastructure depends on microsecond-level timing accuracy.

Article Title: PM Modi received by Uzbek President Mirziyoyev in Tashkent, leaders share car ride

PM Narendra Modi with Uzbekistan Shavkat President Mirziyoyev

PM Modi's 'car' diplomacy

Prime Minister Narendra Modi received a warm and personal welcome from Uzbekistan President Shavkat Mirziyoyev after arriving in capital Tashkent on Saturday for a two-day state visit.From the airport, the two leaders travelled together by car to the presidential palace, marking the latest instance of PM Modi sharing a car ride with a world leader. They held a dinner meeting at the presidential palace.During the visit, the first leg of the prime minister’s two-nation tour, PM Modi will hold delegation-level talks with the Uzbek president to further strengthen the strategic partnership between the two countries.The discussions will cover cooperation in trade and investment, defence, digital connectivity, energy, education and people-to-people ties, while also setting the agenda for future bilateral engagement.In his departure statement, PM Modi noted that the India-Uzbekistan Strategic Partnership had witnessed “significant advancement” in recent years.“I look forward to my discussions with President Mirziyoyev on further deepening our cooperation in trade and investment, digital connectivity, defence, energy, and on advancing our shared visions of Viksit Bharat and Yangi Uzbekistan,” he wrote on X.The visit marks his fourth trip to Uzbekistan since taking office.He previously visited the country in 2015, 2016 and 2022.From Tashkent, PM Modi will travel to Bishkek at the invitation of Kyrgyz President Sadyr Zhaparov to attend the 26th Shanghai Cooperation Organisation (SCO) Summit, which will mark 25 years of the organisation.PM Modi first “carpooled” with a world leader during his 2014 visit to the United States, when he shared a car ride with then-US President Barack Obama.However, since last year, car rides with world leaders have become a recurring feature of what has been described as the prime minister's "informal diplomacy."In September last year, during his visit to China for the SCO Summit, PM Modi travelled in the same car as Vladimir Putin, reciprocating the gesture months later when the Russian president visited New Delhi in December.Since then, he has shared car rides with world leaders including French President Emmanuel Macron, Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz, and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

SRINAGAR: Hurriyat Conference chairman Mirwaiz Umar Farooq Saturday backed National Conference MP Aga Ruhullah Mehdi and criticised the governing party for failing to honour its election promises.He urged all political parties in J&K to raise their voice for the restoration of Article 370 and statehood to the union territory.“I think it is not only Aga Ruhullah Sahib but all political parties, organisations should stand up for the rights of the people and constitutional guarantees,” Mirwaiz told reporters here.While Mirwaiz has consistently spoken about the “rights of the people of J&K,” this is perhaps the first time he has openly criticised the NC for abandoning its position on Article 370 and backed Mehdi, the Srinagar MP who has been vocal in demanding its restoration.Mirwaiz said priorities of the NC govt are different from what it promised to people during the 2024 assembly polls. “The rights of the people have been snatched away, Jammu & Kashmir has been divided, all our legal and constitutional commitments have been completely ignored,” he said.Mirwaiz said electricity, roads and development are important issues which the govt is concerned with. “But I think these are secondary issues.The real issue is that the very existence of the people of Jammu & Kashmir is under threat. At this juncture, all political parties in J&K should not only raise their voice for the restoration of statehood but also seek the restoration of Article 370, which was the basis accession (with India),” Mirwaiz said.He said all promises made to people of J&K from 1947 onwards by the union govt were subsequently reneged upon, including the constitutional guarantees.On Friday, Mehdi, who is also influential Shia cleric, announced he has decided to resign from both the NC and the Lok Sabha and will formally send his resignation letter to the Lok Sabha Speaker on Nov 3, the 26th death anniversary of his father Aga Syed Mehdi, who was killed by terrorists in an IED blast.Mehdi was responding to the NC president Dr Farooq Abdullah’s statement that he should resign and contest elections on his own rather than criticising the party for giving up on Article 370.Mehdi also shot off a letter to Dr Abdullah. “I am repeatedly sermonized about the impracticality of my political position. But what is Article 370, if not shorthand for the struggle to restore the dignity, honour, constitutional guarantees and liberties of our people? Nearly 65% of Jammu & Kashmir’s population is young, and their future is increasingly uncertain, with no jobs and opportunities. Our land is up for grabs.Our resources benefit everybody but us. Our religious rights, traditions and language face constant pressure. Our environment is being ravaged by illegal deforestation, mining and construction in ecologically fragile zones,” the letter reads.

Article Title: From 'khana bana leti ho' to 'will our lives fit together?' How India's marriage biodata is evolving
Article Text:
(AI image)

The old marriage checklist

khana bana leti ho?

What’s changed, and what hasn’t

From 'fitting in' to 'fitting together'

The other side

Biodata vs person

Poll Vote & Share your view Which aspect do you believe should hold more weight in a biodata? Physical appearance Personality traits Financial status Cultural compatibility 3k+ users shared opinion today 5k+ users already voted today 3k+ users shared opinion today Share Opinion

The old checklist is evolving … slowly

New words, old biases

The big picture

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

Every year, India witnesses a familiar wave - the marriage season. Wedding halls fill up, families revive old contacts, matrimonial apps see a surge, and somewhere between the “ladka kya karta hai?” and “ladki ko kya pasand hai?”, the search for a perfect match begins.India records approximately 10 million marriages a year, or roughly 30,000 weddings a day, according to BiodataPlus.in.Amid the rituals, celebrations and matchmaking conversations comes a quieter ritual: the biodata.What looks like a simple one-page profile is, in fact, a snapshot of a changing India, reflecting what families still look for, what young Indians now expect from a partner and how the idea of a “good match” is being rewritten.For years, a marriage biodata followed an almost predictable template: age, height, complexion, caste, salary and family background.For women, descriptions such as “fair”, “homely” and “well-mannered” were not unusual. For men, a stable job, income, property and family status often carried considerable weight.Recalling her experience, 52-year-old Mamata from Uttar Pradesh, told TOI these factors continue to play a major role in rural areas, although expectations have evolved as one moves towards urban India. “During my time, a few family members used to visit the girl’s family and ask questions about her height, age, hobbies and, most importantly, whether she could cook (). The girl’s family wasn’t really allowed to ask questions to the other side.That used to be a very awkward conversation,” she said.But she sees a clear difference in how the next generation approaches marriage.“My daughter has her own perspective and priorities. If parents of my generation were looking for a match for her, we would consider the factors I mentioned above. But those things may not matter to my daughter because she is working and living abroad,” she said.The difference, then, may not simply be about what appears on a biodata. It is also about who gets to decide what matters.So, has the marriage biodata itself really changed?Not really.Shalini Singh, founder of matchmaking platform Andwemet, believes the format has remained surprisingly similar, even as expectations around marriage have evolved.“Honestly, the biodata format itself hasn't changed much because what needs to change is the mindset of the people creating them. That kind of change is hard, but it's the only way forward. And the people who are willing to evolve their biodata are the ones finding better matches,” she said.Relationship coach Sidhharrth S Kumaar of NumroVani sees the shift less in the document itself and more in its purpose.According to him, the question is gradually moving from “Is this family socially suitable?” to “Can these two individuals realistically build a life together?”He also points to a change in who controls the process. While parents were once the primary custodians of marriage biodatas, individuals are increasingly taking charge of their own profiles and decisions, sometimes with guidance from relationship or matrimonial coaches and even AI.“Parents use the biodata to reduce social uncertainty, while their children use it to reduce relationship uncertainty,” noted Kumaar.That distinction captures one of the biggest changes in the modern marriage search.Verona Matchmaking, another platform TOI spoke to, points to another broader shift: the changing role of courtship itself. Young Indians increasingly want the opportunity to date, spend time together and genuinely get to know each other before deciding to marry. Which was yes- not a case earlier.But there is an interesting contradiction. As people become better at describing exactly what they want in a partner, there is also a risk of becoming too good at filtering people out.Verona Matchmaking therefore emphasises the importance of keeping an open mind during the process. The objective, it suggests, “should not be to find someone who perfectly matches every item on a checklist, but to find someone worth getting to know.”For people currently looking for a partner, the shift is increasingly visible in the questions they ask.Rupali Rani, an account manager at The Reppro who is currently looking for a match, told TOI that financial stability is important but no longer enough. “For me, financial stability is only one part of the picture. I want to know how a person thinks, communicates, treats people and looks at life. I would rather have a good conversation with someone and realise that our values align than tick ten boxes on a biodata and then struggle to have a conversation in real life,” she said.For Rani, the change is particularly visible in what women expect from marriage. “It is now less about ‘Will you fit into my family?’ and more about ‘Will our lives fit together?’” she said.“I would rather have an uncomfortable conversation in the beginning than a comfortable misunderstanding that becomes a problem later. My career, my lifestyle and my independence are important to me. Of course, being in a relationship means making adjustments; both people will have to. But adjustment and compromise are not the same thing,” she added.Data cited by the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) also points to broader changes in women’s lives.In India, efforts to delay girls’ marriage have contributed to a decline in marriages before the age of 18, from 47% in 2006 to 23% in 2019-2021. Over the same period, the proportion of girls completing higher secondary education increased from 34% to 48%.But women aren't the only ones rewriting the rules of modern matchmaking. Men, too, are pushing back against transactional evaluations in search of genuine emotional alignment.Shivam Sharma, who is currently looking for a match, told TOI that questions about his CTC, job, property, family responsibilities and career plans are common, particularly from the prospective bride’s family.He understands why families ask such questions but believes a man's worth should not be reduced to his income or assets.“Someone may have a very high salary or own properties worth crores, but that doesn't guarantee that he will be a good husband, that he will bring happiness to his partner, or that the relationship will be free from dishonesty or conflicts,” he said.Instead, Sharma believes families should also ask about a man’s ambitions, values, work ethic, financial plans and how he views his responsibilities towards his family.He also sees a change in who gets the final say.“Both families may still be involved, but ultimately, the decision is increasingly being left to the two people who are actually going to spend their lives together. I think that is an important and positive change,” he said.Traditional expectations from women, however, have not disappeared. Sharma said terms such as “good family” and “homely” can still influence matchmaking, but personally, he does not consider appearance-based factors such as height or fairness important.“For me, good nature, mutual understanding, compatibility and family values matter much more than someone's appearance,” he said.He also does not expect his future wife to give up her ambitions, friendships, interests or individuality after marriage.“If she wants to travel, spend time with her friends, watch a movie, go on a long drive or pursue something that makes her happy, I don't think marriage should stop her from doing those things. She should have her own space and freedom, just as I would expect to have mine,” he said.Major decisions, including family planning, should also be discussed and taken jointly, he added.“Marriage should involve adjustments from both sides, not sacrifices expected from only one person,” Sharma said.For those who have gone through matchmaking, the importance of a biodata can look different in hindsight. What seems important while searching for a partner may not always matter once two people begin building a life together.Vaibhavi Srivastava, an assistant account manager in corporate communications and PR, and Prakhar Mathur, a software test engineer, are now married. Speaking to TOI, they shared what they looked for in each other's biodatas and how their idea of a “good match” has evolved.Srivastava focused more on the individual than the family. She looked for educational qualifications, career, future plans and a progressive, open-minded partner who would support her ambitions. A relatively small family was also a preference.Mathur initially considered age, but soon focused on personality, education and career goals. He liked that Srivastava had “her own goals and clear ideas regarding her future”.For both, compatibility and mutual support mattered more than ticking boxes. Srivastava now places greater emphasis on family values and communication, while Mathur believes biodatas reveal only so much.“Real priorities will come to the fore during a conversation about your way of communication and your view of life,” he said.Neither considered caste or family status deciding factors. Ultimately, they said, the relationship is between the two people getting married.Yet the shift towards compatibility does not mean the traditional marriage checklist has disappeared. Caste, complexion, height, income and family background continue to influence partner selection, though their importance varies across families and generations.Sharma believes caste still matters, but the barrier is thinner than it was for his parents' generation. Greater interaction through education, workplaces and social circles, he said, has made young people more open to cross-caste relationships.“I don't think caste has disappeared, but I do think compatibility, understanding and individual choice are becoming more important,” he said, adding that marriage decisions are increasingly about the two people rather than their caste backgrounds.Rani sees a similar transition. Preferences for someone “fair”, “homely” or from a “good family” remain, she said, even as others prioritise stable careers, emotional maturity and shared values.“We are in a transition phase. The old checklist hasn't disappeared; it has simply started sharing space with a new one,” she said.Ankur Gola, a resident of Delhi, who recently got married, told TOI, “my family was on board with whoever I'm considering but there was an orthodox condition that person should not be of lower cast or muslim; which was difficult for me to accept as they never taught me to discriminate against people... I decided to break the cycle.”Sidhharrth Kumaar takes the argument a step further. He believes traditional factors have not necessarily disappeared, they have sometimes simply been given newer names.Caste, he said, may be described as “cultural compatibility” or “similar traditions”. Complexion and appearance may become “presentable”, “well-groomed” or “fitness-conscious”, while family status may appear as “similar upbringing”, “compatible lifestyle” or “well-settled family”.Even the phrase “our vibes did not match”, he said, can sometimes become a convenient umbrella for discomfort related to appearance, accent, class, caste-coded habits or family culture without explicitly naming the criterion.“These expressions are not inherently discriminatory, but they can camouflage older preferences. The language of matchmaking has modernised faster than the underlying selection criteria,” he said.The transition, therefore, is not a clean break from the past.The vocabulary of matchmaking may be changing, but some of the old filters continue to quietly shape who gets considered a “good match”.The traditional one-page marriage biodata is no longer confined to a printed sheet passed between relatives, family friends or neighbours.Increasingly, matchmaking has moved online, with profiles becoming searchable, editable and instantly shareable.That has changed the reach of the biodata.What once travelled through a limited family or community network can now be shared far beyond it, sometimes with hundreds or thousands of potential matches.Yet technology has not necessarily erased tradition.Instead, the old checklist has found a new home online.A profile can still ask about caste, family, profession and income, even as it increasingly includes interests, lifestyle, career aspirations and expectations from a partner.The format has become digital. The conversation around it is becoming more personal.And perhaps that is the real evolution of the Indian marriage biodata.It is no longer only asking, “Is this person suitable for our family?”Increasingly, the question is becoming:“Can these two people build a life that works for both of them?”The biodata may still fit on one page. But the definition of a “good match” is getting much bigger.
Article Summary: India records approximately 10 million marriages a year, or roughly 30,000 weddings a day, according to BiodataPlus.in. For years, a marriage biodata followed an almost predictable template: age, height, complexion, caste, salary and family background. For women, descriptions such as “fair”, “homely” and “well-mannered” were not unusual. For men, a stable job, income, property and family status often carried considerable weight.

Article Title: August rainfall fails to reduce India's monsoon deficit
Article Text:
Erratic distribution leads to 2% dip in acreage of kharif crops

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Better-than-expected rainfall in many parts of the country in August has failed to reduce India's cumulative monsoon rainfall deficit. While the country's cumulative rainfall deficit (since June 1) was 13% as of July 31, it touched nearly 14% a month later due to a huge shortfall in Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and some northeastern states.This deficit led to an acreage gap in the sowing of kharif (summer-sown) crops, with paddy, the major seasonal crop, reporting a decline of more than 3% compared with the corresponding period last year.Maize that contributes the most as feedstock for ethanol production in the country reported an even bigger decline of more than 4% compared with the corresponding period in 2025. This may eventually create pressure for sugarcane to be used as feedstock for ethanol production.The acreage of all kharif crops, taken together, was reportedly down nearly 2% as of Friday compared with the corresponding period last year. The acreage deficit was nearly 3% at the end of July.The acreage could not be increased due to erratic distribution of rainfall in both the key monsoon months of July and Aug.Though many parts of the country defied El Nino-linked predictions and got normal rainfall, 12 states have reported a rain deficit of more than 20% since June 1, with Bihar, Andhra Pradesh and three northeastern states - Meghalaya, Manipur and Arunachal Pradesh - reporting a huge deficit of more than 40% in cumulative (June 1-Aug 29) rainfall.El Nino is a climatic condition which sees the warming of surface waters of the central and eastern tropical Pacific Ocean. It is associated with weak monsoons and harsher summers in India.Good rains in eastern India during the remaining two days of the month, as predicted by IMD, may slightly reduce the deficit for the region, but it won't help much overall, as the Met department Saturday predicted the continuation of "subdued rainfall activity" over peninsular India during the next week.Peninsular India has, so far, reported a deficit of more than 23% in cumulative rainfall, leaving Andhra Pradesh, Karnataka and Kerala largely dry for most of the southwest (summer) monsoon season. Predicting good rains in the east for the next two-three days, IMD said isolated "heavy to very heavy rainfall" is likely over Gangetic West Bengal on Sunday, Jharkhand on Monday and Odisha till Sept 1 due to the "influence of low-pressure area over northwest Bay of Bengal and adjoining West Bengal-north Odisha coasts".
Article Summary: Better-than-expected rainfall in many parts of the country in August has failed to reduce India's cumulative monsoon rainfall deficit. Bihar, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab and some northeastern states reported a huge deficit of more than 40% since June 1. This deficit led to an acreage gap in the sowing of kharif (summer-sown) crops.

Article Title: 'RSS vision is to see the world as one': Sangh chief Mohan Bhagwat at New York event
Article Text:
'Unity in diversity in Bharat's DNA: RSS chief Mohan Bhagwat

‘Be true to America’: RSS chief message to diaspora

Highlights responsibility towards others

Bhagwat offers interpretation of Dharma

Join conversation View All Comments → Share your thoughts in the comments Insightful Agree Disagree Skeptical Concerning Promising Worth Reading Big Development Post Comment Be respectful · TOI community guidelines

NEW DELHI: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat , addressing around 5,000 members of Indian-American organisations at Madison Square Garden in New York, spoke about unity, pluralism, individual responsibility and the obligations of the Indian diaspora, while arguing that material success alone cannot define a fulfilling life.Bhagwat was speaking at the “Universal Oneness Celebration”, organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue. He framed his address around the idea of “oneness”, drawing parallels between the pluralism associated with the United States and what he described as Bharat’s “unity in diversity”.“When we say America, United States of America, one word is often discussed frequently. That is pluralism,” Bhagwat said. “And when we say Bharat, another word, another phrase is discussed: unity in diversity.”“For Bharat, this unity and diversity, both are in their DNA,” he said.Bhagwat said differences between people were a natural feature of life, but argued that these differences existed alongside an underlying sense of oneness.“So many styles of living. We appear different. We are different,” he said, pointing to differences in people's everyday needs and circumstances.“But there is innate oneness. That is why we feel for each other,” he added.He described diversity as the “decoration of oneness”, presenting unity not as the absence of differences but as something that exists beneath them.Bhagwat also linked this idea to what he described as the responsibilities of individuals, societies and nations. Nations, he said, should not be seen merely as geographical entities but as having a larger purpose.“These nations are not merely geographical entities. In the design of this universe, nations have to carry out a duty,” he said, quoting Swami Vivekananda's formulation that every nation has a message, a mission and a destiny.Turning to the Indian diaspora in the United States, Bhagwat said Indians living abroad had a primary responsibility towards the country where they lived and worked.“So we are Americans, and we should be true to America,” he said.He described this as a duty towards one's “karma bhumi” — the land where a person lives and works.“The diaspora, Indian diaspora, they have a duty to their karma bhumi. They must fulfill that. They should be loyal to their karma bhumi,” Bhagwat said.At the same time, he said Indians abroad could maintain a connection with Bharat as their “janma bhumi”, or birthplace, and could contribute to the country if they wished to do so after fulfilling their responsibilities to their adopted home.“But it is not obligatory,” he said.Instead, he said, the connection with Bharat should be reflected in the values carried by the diaspora.“Your janma bhumi expects you to live the values it has imparted on you,” Bhagwat said.Bhagwat also questioned the idea that professional success should be measured primarily through earnings and material possessions.“How much we earn is not important. How much we distribute is important,” he said.He asked whether a career could be reduced to money and material happiness, while acknowledging that material aspirations had a legitimate place in Hindu philosophy.“You think of career? Is career only money? Is career only material happiness?” Bhagwat asked.He referred to the four Purusharthas, saying that Artha and Kama represented important material dimensions of life alongside spiritual pursuits.“It is not denied. In four Purusharthas, Artha and Kama are two important Purusharthas related to material life,” he said.Bhagwat also referred to the traditional four stages of life — Brahmacharya, Grihastha, Vanaprastha and Sannyasa — arguing that people acquire different responsibilities as they move through life.“So you have to learn, you have to sustain life, and you have to give the advice, your experience to next generation,” he said.He argued that material abundance by itself could not guarantee fulfilment.“So the material happiness is transient, cannot satisfy,” Bhagwat said. “And if abundance of material happiness is there, it may fail also. And therefore there is no satisfaction.”Bhagwat's broader argument centred on the idea that human intelligence carried with it a responsibility towards others.Using the example of a hungry person watching someone eat, he said people instinctively recognise another person's suffering and cannot simply ignore it.“A simple experiment you can do, or I can challenge you to do. When you are taking your lunch or dinner, let a hungry man stand before you, and let him stare at your full platter with hungry eyes,” he said.“You can try; you will not do. Because we are human beings.”He contrasted human beings' ability to think and plan with the instinctive behaviour of animals, but said the ability to think also brought a responsibility to use that capacity correctly.“If you think in the right way, you go nearer to God. If you think in the wrong way, you go nearer to the animal kingdom,” he said.Bhagwat also offered a broader interpretation of “Dharma”, saying it should not be understood simply as religion or worship.“Dharma is not religion. It is not worship. It is beyond all this,” he said.He described Dharma as a sustaining principle that allows people and society to manage competing aspects of life and maintain balance.“It is the balance which sustains everything at once, simultaneously, and simultaneously everyone can progress,” Bhagwat said.He similarly argued that progress should not require either individuals or society to be suppressed.“Individual, society and environment, they have to proceed together, progress together,” he said, adding that different aspects of an individual's own life — body, mind and intellect — also had to advance together.Bhagwat concluded by returning to the idea of responsibility towards both one's place of work and birthplace.He called on people to fulfil their duties towards their “karma bhumi” as well as their “janma bhumi”, saying such an approach could help a world struggling with multiple challenges.“To that destiny and fulfill our duties in our karma bhumi as well as our janma bhumi,” he said.“If we do that, that will be a boon for the world struggling with all these problems and stumbling at every step.”
Article Summary: Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh ( RSS ) chief Mohan Bhagwat spoke about unity, pluralism, individual responsibility and the obligations of the Indian diaspora. He was speaking at the “Universal Oneness Celebration’, organised by American Hindus for Engagement and Dialogue.

NEW DELHI: BJP president Nitin Nabin Saturday reprimanded three Delhi MPs - Ramvir Singh Bidhuri, Yogender Chandolia and Kamaljeet Sehrawat - for visiting the residence of anti-Sikh riot convict Sajjan Kumar, who died Aug 20, to pay their condolences.The move comes amid the party's preparations for the Punjab assembly elections.Kumar was a serving life sentence in two cases for his role in the 1984 riots and died of illness at 80 years of age.BJP sources said the three MPs were summoned to meet Nabin.
